n: Nephi begins quoting Isaiah 2–14 (2 Nephi 12–24). Isaiah, son of Amoz, prophesied in Jerusalem about 740–700 BC, during the rise of Assyria. This heading introduces a vision about Judah and Jerusalem.

In the last days, the “mountain of the Lord’s house” — His temple — will be raised above all hills, and all nations will stream to it. Latter-day Saints see fulfillment in temples, including those in the Rocky Mountains, and in a future temple in Jerusalem.

f.w: the mountain of the Lord's house

n: People will invite each other to go up to God’s house to learn His ways. His law will go out from Zion and His word from Jerusalem — two centers of God’s work.

f.w: he will teach us of his ways
out of Zion shall go forth the law

n: The Lord will judge the nations. Weapons will be turned into farm tools, and war will end — the peace of the Millennium.

f.w: they shall beat their swords into plow-shares

n: Isaiah calls Israel to walk in the Lord’s light. The Book of Mormon adds, “yea, come, for ye have all gone astray, every one to his wicked ways” — not in the KJV.
Isaiah turns to Judah’s sins: they have filled up with foreign eastern practices and follow fortune-tellers like the Philistines, embracing foreign ways and alliances.

f.g: Fortune-tellers who claim to predict the future.

f.w: please themselves in the children of strangers
f.g: Make deals or alliances with foreigners.

n: The land is full of silver, gold, horses, and chariots. Israel’s kings were warned not to multiply these, since trust in wealth and military power replaces trust in God.
The land is also full of idols. People worship what their own hands have made.

f.w: they worship the work of their own hands

n: The Book of Mormon reads that neither the lowly (“mean man”) nor the great humble themselves — the KJV says they do bow down (to idols). Either way, pride and idolatry prevent forgiveness.
The wicked will try to hide in rocks and dust from the terror of the Lord’s glory. The Book of Mormon adds “O ye wicked ones.”
Human pride will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day.

f.w: the Lord alone shall be exalted

n: The day of the Lord is coming upon all nations and every proud person. The Book of Mormon expands this verse, stressing that it will come soon and on everyone.

f.w: the day of the Lord of Hosts

n: It will come upon the tall cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan — famous majestic trees symbolizing proud people and nations.

f.g: Prized tall trees used in Solomon’s temple.
A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, known for oaks and cattle.

n: It will come upon high mountains and hills, and — the Book of Mormon adds — upon proud nations and every people.
Every high tower and fortified wall — symbols of human security — will be brought low.

The day of the Lord will also humble trading ships and their luxuries. Scholars have noticed that the Book of Mormon includes both “ships of the sea” (found in the ancient Greek Septuagint) and “ships of Tarshish” (in the Hebrew), as if preserving a fuller original line.

f.g: Large merchant ships for long voyages; Tarshish was a distant trading port, perhaps in Spain.

n: Human pride will be bowed down, and the Lord alone will be exalted — a refrain repeated from verse 11.
God will completely abolish idols.

f.w: the idols he shall utterly abolish

n: People will flee into caves when the Lord rises to shake the earth — imagery associated with the Second Coming.
People will throw their silver and gold idols to the moles and bats — leaving them in dark holes, seeing their worthlessness at last.

f.w: to the moles and to the bats

n: They will hide in the clefts of rugged rocks when the Lord shakes the earth.
Stop trusting in mortal man, whose life is only a breath. What is he really worth compared to God?

f.w: whose breath is in his nostrils
